units.title: Natural, whole numbers and integers
units.key_idea: Natural numbers start at 1, whole numbers add 0, and integers also include negative numbers.
units.body:
When you count goats in a herd, you say 1, 2, 3, 4... These counting numbers are called natural numbers.

If there are no goats in the shed, the count is 0. When we add 0 to the natural numbers we get whole numbers: 0, 1, 2, 3...

Now think about money. If you have ₹50 and you borrow ₹80 from a shopkeeper, after paying everything you are ₹30 short. We write this as −30. Numbers like −1, −2, −3 are negative numbers.

Integers are all whole numbers together with their negatives: ... −3, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, 3 ...

We can show them on a number line. Draw a line, mark 0 in the middle. Positive numbers go to the right, negative numbers to the left. A number further right is always bigger. So −2 is bigger than −5, just as being ₹2 short is better than being ₹5 short.

So: every natural number is a whole number, and every whole number is an integer.

units.title: Rational numbers
units.key_idea: A rational number can be written as p/q, where p and q are integers and q is not zero.
units.body:
If you cut a roti into 4 equal parts and eat 1, you ate 1/4 of the roti. Numbers like 1/4, 3/2 and −5/7 are fractions.

A rational number is any number that can be written as p/q, where p and q are integers and q is not 0.

Examples:
1. 3/4 is rational.
2. 5 is rational, because 5 = 5/1.
3. −2 is rational, because −2 = −2/1.
4. 0 is rational, because 0 = 0/1.
5. 0.5 is rational, because 0.5 = 1/2.

So every integer is also a rational number.

Why can q not be 0? Because dividing by zero has no meaning. You cannot share 6 mangoes among 0 people.

There are infinitely many rational numbers between any two numbers. Between 1 and 2 you can find 3/2, then between 1 and 3/2 you can find 5/4, and so on, forever. A simple trick: the average of two numbers always lies between them.

When you write a rational number as a decimal, it either stops (1/4 = 0.25) or repeats a pattern (1/3 = 0.333...).
questions: A rational number can be written in the form:
p/q with q not equal to 0
Rational numbers are ratios of integers with a non-zero denominator.
No, it is a whole number only
Every integer n can be written as n/1.
Why can q not be 0 in p/q?
Division by zero has no meaning
We cannot divide anything into zero parts.
Which is a rational number between 1 and 2?
How many rational numbers are there between 1 and 2?
We can always find another rational number between any two.
−2/7 is a ratio of integers, so it is rational.

units.title: Irrational and real numbers
units.key_idea: Irrational numbers cannot be written as p/q; their decimals never stop and never repeat. Rational and irrational together make real numbers.
units.body:
Some numbers cannot be written as p/q at all. These are called irrational numbers.

A famous one is √2. Draw a square field that is 1 metre on each side. The diagonal from one corner to the opposite corner is √2 metres long. Its decimal is 1.41421356... It never ends and never repeats.

Another famous irrational number is π (pi). It is the ratio of the distance around a circle to its width. If you measure the rope around a round well and divide by the well's width, you get about 3.14. In fact π = 3.14159... and it goes on forever without a pattern. We often use 22/7 as an approximate value, but π is not exactly 22/7.

How to tell them apart:
1. Decimal stops or repeats → rational.
2. Decimal goes on forever without repeating → irrational.

All rational and irrational numbers together are called real numbers. Every real number has exactly one point on the number line, and every point on the line is a real number.

units.title: Equations with two unknowns
units.key_idea: An equation like ax + by + c = 0 has two unknowns, x and y, and many possible solutions.
units.body:
At the weekly haat, a pen costs ₹x and a notebook costs ₹y. Meena pays ₹40 for 2 pens and 1 notebook. We can write:

2x + y = 40

This is a linear equation in two variables. Any equation that can be written as ax + by + c = 0, where a and b are not both zero, is of this type. Here a = 2, b = 1 and c = −40.

A solution is a pair of values (x, y) that makes the equation true. Let's try:
1. If a pen costs ₹10, then 2(10) + y = 40, so y = 20. The pair (10, 20) works.
2. If a pen costs ₹15, then y = 10. The pair (15, 10) also works.
3. If a pen costs ₹5, then y = 30. The pair (5, 30) works too.

So a linear equation in two variables has many solutions, in fact infinitely many. To find one, pick any value for x and calculate y.

To check a solution, put the values into the equation and see if both sides are equal.
questions: Which is a linear equation in two variables?
It has two variables, each to the power 1.
How many solutions does 2x + y = 40 have?
Each value of x gives a matching y, so there are endless solutions.

units.title: Drawing the graph of an equation
units.key_idea: The graph of a linear equation in two variables is a straight line, and every point on it is a solution.
units.body:
We can draw a picture of an equation on graph paper. Take x + y = 5.

Step 1: Make a small table of solutions.
• x = 0 → y = 5, point (0, 5)
• x = 2 → y = 3, point (2, 3)
• x = 5 → y = 0, point (5, 0)

Step 2: Draw the x-axis (across) and the y-axis (up). Mark each point. For (2, 3), go 2 steps right and 3 steps up.

Step 3: Join the points with a ruler. They lie on one straight line!

The graph of every linear equation in two variables is a straight line. That is why it is called "linear".

Every point on the line is a solution, and every solution is a point on the line. For example, (1, 4) is on the line and 1 + 4 = 5. The point (3, 3) is not on the line, and 3 + 3 = 6, not 5.

Two points are enough to draw a line, but we plot three to check we made no mistake. If the three points are not in a line, recheck your table.

units.title: Equations from real life
units.key_idea: Turn a word problem into an equation by naming the unknowns as x and y, then writing the rule as ax + by = c.
units.body:
Many daily situations can be written as linear equations.

Example 1: A farmer has hens and goats. Together they have 20 legs. A hen has 2 legs and a goat has 4. If x is the number of hens and y the number of goats:
2x + 4y = 20
Solutions include (2, 4), (4, 3), (6, 2), (10, 0).

Example 2: Auto fare in a town is ₹10 for the first km and ₹8 for every km after that. If total distance is x km and fare is ₹y:
y = 10 + 8(x − 1), which simplifies to y = 8x + 2.

Example 3: Two friends together saved ₹100. If Asha saved x and Bunty saved y:
x + y = 100.

Steps for any word problem:
1. Decide what x and y stand for. Write it down.
2. Find the rule that connects them.
3. Write the equation.
4. Check it with one easy example.

In real life, values like the number of goats must be whole numbers, so we only accept sensible solutions.
